frames.narration: A viewer types "what a goal!" and sends it. The phone's WebSocket ends at gateway 17, which holds about 50,000 connections. The gateway does no checks of its own, it passes the comment to the ingest service.

Ingest checks the session, applies the per-user rate limit, runs the blocklist and the toxicity score, and gives the comment the next sequence number. It is appended to the durable log, so it is never lost even if everything after this fails.

About 2,778 comments arrive this second, and a sampler keeps only 10 for the whole stream. Priority is a fixed hash of the comment id, so this comment either wins its second or does not, on every node alike. It wins, and is published once to the stream's topic.

The topic hands the message to the relay tier. Each relay serves 10 gateways, so 10 relays reach all 100 gateways. Each gateway then writes the same 10 comments to its own 50,000 phones. Nothing sends to 5 million phones from one place.

The goal makes people tap hearts. Gateway 17 sees about 500 taps in this second, and instead of forwarding each one it adds them to four counters in memory and sends the totals as a single small tally.

The counters add the tallies from all 100 gateways: 24,990 hearts, 12,540 laughs, 9,980 claps and 2,502 wows, which is 50,012 taps in the second. Addition does not depend on the order in which tallies arrive, and the tally is published as 4 numbers.

The tally goes down the same tree as the comments, so every phone gets one tiny message per second. The phone draws a burst of floating hearts sized by the number, not one animation per tap. The viewer sees the comment and the reactions about a second after the goal.

Another viewer is on a poor network and reads only 5 messages per second. Gateway 17 keeps a queue of at most 50 for this connection, drops the oldest comments when it fills, and always keeps the newest tally. One slow phone cannot grow the gateway's memory.
